segments.title: When rational interests leave no compromise
segments.body: The episode distinguishes wars driven by bad actors, wars that remain tragic despite reasonable choices, and wars born of folly. Copenhagen is placed in the second category at the close. Britain considered its blockade, access to Baltic naval stores, and protection against a French-aligned coalition vital. Denmark-Norway risked war whether it chose Britain or the Franco-Russian side. Each state's acceptable outcome was intolerable to the other, leaving no workable compromise.

evidence.note: The opening distinguishes wars driven by bad actors, tragic collisions of reasonable choices, and folly.
The closing identifies Copenhagen as a conflict in which national interests left no acceptable compromise.

segments.summary: Copenhagen shows how states pursuing understandable national interests can still reach war when no acceptable compromise remains.

segments.title: A war aimed at breaking the League
segments.body: Britain saw the League as protection for French interests while it was already at war with France and Spain. The operation pursued a limited political objective rather than Danish territory. Its purpose was to break the maritime coalition before its fleets and economic pressure could reinforce Britain's enemies. The 1801 crisis was naval diplomacy backed by force, with combat used to secure a negotiated result.

evidence.note: The introduction identifies the attack and the League of Armed Neutrality as the cause of the conflict.

segments.summary: The Copenhagen operation was a British attempt to break the Second League of Armed Neutrality through a limited coercive campaign.

segments.title: Denmark-Norway's impossible strategic choice
segments.body: Denmark-Norway could appear to choose Britain and risk pressure or invasion from France and Russia, or join the league and provoke Britain. Crown Prince Frederick understood that either course could lead to war, yet Denmark did not fully mobilize its fleet, fortify Copenhagen, or summon allied forces forward. Its capital's position beside the Danish straits made that indecision unusually consequential. Baltic access mattered to fleets, commerce, and coalition strategy, so Denmark-Norway could not behave as though its alignment were a purely diplomatic choice.

evidence.note: Frederick's choices and Copenhagen's strategic position.

segments.summary: Crown Prince Frederick faced pressure from France and Russia on one side and Britain on the other, with Copenhagen controlling the Baltic approaches.

segments.title: Neutral convoys, blockade, and Baltic naval stores
segments.body: Britain treated neutral convoys carrying French ships or goods as a practical threat to its blockade and prize-court system. British warships normally detained doubtful vessels and let prize courts decide whether ships or cargoes should be released. Denmark and other neutral powers instead claimed that their convoy protection should prevent British searches, even when French-flagged ships or French-bound goods were involved. The problem became more acute because Scandinavian naval stores were vital to British sea power. A league that could shelter enemy commerce, weaken the blockade, and restrict naval supplies was therefore not merely a legal argument about neutral flags. The passage also looks ahead to the later English Wars, when the danger that France might take or direct the Danish fleet again put British access to Baltic supplies at issue.

evidence.note: Neutral-convoy claims could shelter French ships and goods from British blockade searches, while Scandinavian naval stores made League control of Baltic commerce a material threat that returned during the later English Wars.

segments.summary: The dispute joined neutral-convoy rights to Britain's need to inspect commerce, maintain its blockade, and secure Scandinavian supplies for the Royal Navy.

segments.title: Why the League could fall like dominoes
segments.body: Catherine II's earlier league had considered the seasonal rhythm of northern fleets and arranged its pressure when the members could support one another. The Second League formed as winter was closing the northern Baltic bases. Denmark's waters opened sooner than Russia's, leaving the smallest exposed member reachable before the stronger Russian fleet was free of ice. That transformed a supposed united front into a sequence of separate targets. Britain could strike the first domino and use the resulting momentum to weaken the whole coalition.

evidence.note: Comparison of the timing of the first and second leagues; the domino logic.

segments.summary: The earlier league worked around fleet movements and winter ice; the 1800 version left Denmark exposed before stronger Baltic fleets could act together.

segments.title: Paul I and the posthumous coronation of Peter III
segments.body: Paul I revered his father, Peter III, whose death remained surrounded by competing explanations. He idealized Peter and made that filial devotion part of imperial ceremony. After Catherine died, Paul had Peter's buried body exhumed, placed the imperial crown on the remains, and arranged a new burial. The episode conveys the intensity of Paul's reverence for a father he had turned into a political and personal ideal. It also provides context for the ruler who later assembled the Second League.

evidence.note: Paul I's veneration of Peter III led him to exhume, posthumously crown, and rebury his father's remains, revealing the dynastic fixation of the ruler who later formed the Second League.

segments.summary: Paul I's posthumous coronation and reburial of Peter III reveal the dynastic fixation of the ruler who formed the Second League of Armed Neutrality.

segments.title: Tsar Paul turns neutrality into a coalition threat
segments.body: The league brought Russia, Denmark-Norway, Prussia, and Sweden together during the War of the Second Coalition. Its members could present it as protection for neutral commerce, but Tsar Paul I also aligned Russia with France. Britain's leaders consequently saw Russian policy as linked to their French enemy rather than as impartial protection of shipping. The coalition also threatened British access to Baltic supplies. That combination explains why London treated the league as a potential hostile naval bloc rather than a detached legal arrangement.

evidence.note: Russia, Denmark-Norway, Prussia, and Sweden formed the Second League of Armed Neutrality, but Paul I's alignment with France made Britain view it as a hostile naval bloc rather than an impartial commercial league.

segments.summary: The Second League of Armed Neutrality included Russia, Denmark-Norway, Prussia and Sweden, but Paul I's alignment with France undermined its claim to neutrality.

segments.title: The fleet as diplomatic cover
segments.body: The British approach mixed coercion with a proposed settlement over convoy rules. A smaller mission in August 1800 had opened talks with Denmark, and London hoped to extend agreed rules to Sweden and other Baltic states. The visible fleet also gave Denmark-Norway a possible explanation for making concessions under pressure rather than appearing voluntarily to abandon France and Russia. It demonstrated that Britain could support states threatened around the Baltic and could complicate reinforcement across the sea. Armies campaigning in Europe's grain-rich regions could forage more easily than northern garrisons facing shorter growing seasons, smaller surpluses, and dependent families and support units. That food and sustainment burden made a large continental intervention less straightforward and increased the diplomatic value of a mobile fleet.

evidence.note: The 1800 mission, diplomatic intent, and the logistical limits on a French land intervention.

segments.summary: Britain first used a fleet to press for an agreement, hoping its presence would give Denmark-Norway room to disengage from French and Russian pressure.

segments.title: The race before the Baltic thaw
segments.body: Great Yarmouth gave the assembled British fleet useful options toward the Netherlands, the Baltic, or the Channel, while the selected second and third rates left first rates on more critical duties. The potential combined fleet shaped British planning even if the largest estimate of 123 ships of the line was a worst-case scenario. A much smaller Baltic concentration of forty or fifty ships could still become dangerous if it joined Dutch forces or acted while Franco-Spanish fleets pressed from the south. London feared losing control of the Channel under simultaneous pressure. Britain also wanted to act before French or Russian troops reinforced Denmark. Striking the league while its fleets and armies remained divided was therefore the operational logic behind the race against the thaw.

evidence.note: The Yarmouth staging choice, force selection, ice-bound Russian fleet, and danger of combined Baltic forces.

segments.summary: Britain had to act before ice released Russian ships that could combine with Swedish and Danish forces into a formidable Baltic fleet.

segments.title: Parker's diplomacy and Nelson's fighting role
segments.body: Hyde Parker's methodical temperament and obedience to orders contrasted with Horatio Nelson's forceful operational style. Parker suited a campaign intended to leave time for negotiation and let League members reconsider their position. Nelson, the victor of the Nile, supplied the aggressive fighting capacity if diplomacy failed. Placing Parker in overall command kept the limited political aim prominent. Making Nelson second-in-command ensured that the fleet still had a commander able to force the issue at Copenhagen.

evidence.note: Hyde Parker's methodical obedience suited a controlled diplomatic campaign, while Nelson supplied aggressive fighting capacity as second-in-command if negotiation failed.

segments.summary: Hyde Parker was selected for a controlled, diplomatic campaign while Nelson supplied the aggressive fighting capacity if diplomacy failed.

segments.title: Collingwood, Duncan, and models of admiralship
segments.body: The Parker-Nelson comparison opens a wider aside about what makes a naval officer worth studying. Collingwood is offered as the preferred model for a modern naval professional. Duncan remains a favourite, although the harsh personal discipline in his mutiny anecdote makes him a less transferable example. The leading age-of-sail group also includes Nelson, Jervis, and Rodney, while the broader list reaches Vian, Henderson, Cunningham, Jellicoe, and Hornby. Naval leadership may rest on combat command or on the quieter work of institutional preparation and professional example.

evidence.note: Collingwood and Duncan compared as professional models, alongside a wider group of leading British admirals.

segments.summary: The Parker-Nelson comparison opens a wider reflection on why admirals may deserve study for different kinds of professional achievement.

segments.title: Danish command misreads Britain's objective
segments.body: Denmark's command appointments and planning did not match the opponent or the political problem. Against Nelson, the victor of the Nile, much of the Danish fleet was converted into stationary batteries without a clear plan for the remaining mobile ships. Steen Bille's precise influence on this arrangement is left uncertain, despite his later role in Denmark's gunboat strategy during the English Wars. Britain's limited objective was to clear a route for bomb vessels, threaten Copenhagen, and compel Denmark-Norway to leave the League. Preserving an untouched northern force while the southern defence bore the decisive attack failed to contest that operation.

evidence.note: The lecture critiques Danish command choices, identifies the bomb-vessel objective, and explains the intended diplomatic domino effect.

segments.summary: Denmark's commanders prepared a harbour battle without centring the British requirement to move bomb vessels within range of Copenhagen and break the League.

segments.title: From Denmark to Sweden, Prussia, and Russia
segments.body: The domino plan depended on diplomacy as well as thaw dates and fleet geography. If Copenhagen compelled Denmark-Norway to leave the League, British access to the Baltic could make Sweden reconsider without another full battle. Prussia presented a different problem, one suited to the familiar coalition model of British money funding Prussian soldiers. Russia remained the largest final obstacle, but its fleet might still be divided and many of its officers understood Royal Navy capabilities firsthand. The operation tried to turn one limited victory into a succession of easier diplomatic and military choices.

evidence.note: Britain expected Denmark-Norway's withdrawal to make Sweden reconsider, planned to combine British subsidies with Prussian soldiers in the familiar coalition model, and treated Russia as the final and largest obstacle.

segments.summary: Britain expected pressure on Denmark to reshape the choices facing Sweden and Prussia before any final confrontation with Russia.

segments.title: Denmark's static defence and unused mobile ships
segments.body: The Danish plan combined moored ships, floating batteries, shore batteries, and a small group of vessels kept rigged and ready for sea. In theory, the mobile force could wait until Nelson's ships anchored and then attack individual British vessels from the other side, reproducing the double-sided pressure used at the Nile. No such sortie took place. Command changes, uncertainty over who should lead it, and the decision to keep the reserve facing Parker's northern division left Nelson's flank unchallenged. Coordinated use of the available ships could have made the attack far harder or even physically impossible in its chosen form.

evidence.note: The Danish battery system and the unrealized opportunity for mobile ships to attack Nelson's anchored line.

segments.summary: Danish ships and batteries created a formidable-looking harbour defence, but command arrangements left mobile ships unused when a flanking attack might have mattered.

segments.title: A limited British squadron with a coercive mission
segments.body: Parker retained two second rates and six third rates in the northern reserve while Nelson took twelve nominal ships of the line into the southern channel. Three of Nelson's ships grounded, so only nine reached the attack. The force included 64-gun ships and two smaller fourth rates rather than an overwhelming concentration of Britain's newest capital ships. Seven bomb vessels supplied the main coercive leverage, supported by frigates and smaller craft. The squadron also included fire ships, which appear here as an unusual addition rather than the decisive arm. Bringing the bomb vessels within range of Copenhagen could turn a limited tactical success into direct political pressure on the Danish government.

evidence.note: Only nine of Nelson's twelve nominal ships of the line reached the attack after three grounded, while seven bomb vessels supplied the leverage to turn tactical success into direct pressure on Copenhagen.

segments.summary: Britain relied on a limited attacking squadron whose bomb vessels could turn tactical success into direct pressure on Copenhagen.

segments.title: Denmark's unused strength and training gap
segments.body: British victory owed as much to Denmark-Norway's failure to use available resources as to British skill. Fourteen modern ships under Steen Bille and a similar number of smaller vessels remained in harbour, while Crown Prince Frederick's command system persisted with a failing plan. Volunteers with little or no naval experience were rowed out to reinforce battered floating batteries against Royal Navy crews accustomed to large-scale action. Danish frigates had fought ferociously in earlier convoy clashes, but courage in small actions could not supply the practiced coordination required in a mass fleet battle. Patriotic enthusiasm and martial ancestry could not replace repeated training, clear command arrangements, and institutional preparation.

evidence.note: Comparison of Denmark-Norway's unused ships and brave convoy fighting with command indecision and the training needed for a mass fleet action.

segments.summary: Denmark-Norway's command indecision and lack of fleet-action training mattered more than any shortage of courage or available ships.

segments.title: Nelson's southern anchoring attack
segments.body: The Danish defence expected the principal attack from the north, but Nelson approached through the southern channel after inspecting the difficult waters. Each British ship sailed past the vessels already engaged and anchored by the stern opposite the next Danish position. This brought the line into action successively without allowing it to overextend. The effect resembled a walking barrage moving up the defensive line. The navigation remained hazardous: Agamemnon, Russell, and Bellona grounded before they could take their intended places.

evidence.note: The unexpected southern approach, successive anchoring and three grounded British ships.

segments.summary: Nelson approached from the south rather than the expected north, anchoring ships successively opposite the Danish line to concentrate fire without overextending his force.

segments.title: A failing shore-to-ship reinforcement system
segments.body: The fleets anchored roughly a cable apart and exchanged broadsides, leaving little room for manoeuvre once the line was formed. Low floating batteries added fire that the British had not fully noticed before the action. Danish reinforcements were rowed from shore batteries to vessels already under heavy fire, reducing the crews available to keep those fixed defences operating. Many boats reached ships only after they were silenced or unable to fight, so the process weakened one position without reliably restoring another. The fully crewed reserve ships to the north remained inactive while Parker's heavier division approached, leaving Nelson's flank unchallenged.

evidence.note: The firefight, shore-to-ship reinforcements and inactive northern Danish ships.

segments.summary: Once the fleets anchored, Denmark weakened its shore batteries to reinforce ships under fire while the fully crewed northern reserve stayed inactive.

segments.title: Isis and Monarch survive concentrated Danish fire
segments.body: At about 1 p.m., Prøvesteenen's fire placed the 50-gun HMS Isis in serious danger. The frigate HMS Désirée raked the Danish position with assistance from HMS Polyphemus, preventing it from finishing Isis. Elsewhere, HMS Monarch was damaged by the combined fire of Holstein and Sjælland. These ship-level episodes show that the Danish line could inflict severe punishment even though its command system failed to coordinate the wider defence. The passage also foreshadows Holstein's later distinction as the only captured Danish vessel retained for British service.

evidence.note: The danger to Isis, Désirée and Polyphemus attacking Prøvesteenen, and Monarch taking fire from Holstein and Sjælland.

segments.summary: Prøvesteenen nearly overwhelmed the 50-gun HMS Isis before HMS Désirée and HMS Polyphemus intervened, while HMS Monarch suffered under concentrated Danish fire.

segments.title: Why Nelson ignored the recall signal
segments.body: Parker saw distress signals from grounded British ships and raised the recall to give Nelson a lawful way to disengage if he could no longer continue. The signal offered discretion rather than an unavoidable order to retreat. Nelson acknowledged it but did not repeat it, making the famous remark about having a right to be blind sometimes. His subordinate Thomas Graves kept Nelson's close-action signal prominent while placing the recall where other ships could not readily see it. Captain Edward Riou, unable to see Nelson's flagship, obeyed Parker literally, withdrew his frigate force past heavier fortress fire, and was killed.

evidence.note: The transcript recounts Parker's signal, Nelson's response, Graves's handling of signals and Riou's withdrawal.

segments.summary: Parker's signal gave Nelson discretion to disengage; Nelson acknowledged it but continued the close action, producing the famous blind-eye episode.

segments.title: From battle to coercive negotiation
segments.body: Experienced British gunnery progressively silenced most of the Danish line by about 2 p.m. The shore batteries had also been depleted by sending their crews out as reinforcements, allowing British bomb vessels to move closer to Copenhagen. Nelson then sent a Danish-speaking officer under a flag of truce to Crown Prince Frederick. His message offered to spare Denmark if resistance ceased but warned that captured floating batteries might otherwise be burned with their defenders aboard. The ensuing exchange produced a 24-hour ceasefire and shifted the operation from battle back to diplomacy. The damaged Danish flagship Dannebrog exploded after the agreement, killing 250 men. Several battered British ships grounded during the withdrawal, so the tactical victory ended with further damage.

evidence.note: The shift in firing, bomb vessels, Nelson's message, the ceasefire, Dannebrog's explosion, and British ships grounding during withdrawal.

segments.summary: As the Danish line fell silent, Nelson brought bomb vessels closer and used a flag of truce to turn naval victory into negotiations with Crown Prince Frederick.

segments.title: Prize-taking amid the silenced Danish line
segments.body: Once much of the Danish line stopped firing, British boats moved in to accept surrenders, help damaged vessels stay afloat, and secure them as prizes. Some positions resumed fire as the boats approached, showing that tactical silence did not produce an orderly end to the action. Two Danish vessels trying to leave together sank, while one frigate successfully withdrew. Commodore Olfert Fischer moved from the burning Dannebrog to Holstein and then to Trekroner after Holstein struck. From the fortress he could still engage damaged British frigates that drifted within range, but these local actions did not reverse the battle.

evidence.note: British boats approaching silenced Danish positions met renewed fire as two vessels sank and one frigate escaped; Olfert Fischer moved his command from burning Dannebrog through Holstein to Trekroner.

segments.summary: British boats approaching silenced positions to accept surrenders and preserve prizes encountered renewed fire while Danish command shifted between ships and Trekroner.

segments.title: The cost of Copenhagen's static defence
segments.body: Danish-Norwegian losses cannot be reconstructed precisely because many volunteers were not consistently recorded before or after the battle. Estimates for those killed, wounded, and captured range from roughly 1,100 to 2,200, while Olfert Fischer put the figure between 1,600 and 1,800. British records list 963 killed and wounded. Patriotic courage could not substitute for trained crews able to load, aim, and fight almost automatically under fire. Two Danish ships sank, one exploded, and twelve were captured. Britain expected that further Baltic fighting might follow and could not spare prize crews, so it burned eleven captured vessels and retained only Holstein, later commissioned as HMS Nassau. Its mixed battery made it a 64-gun ship of limited general utility, but it served in selected missions and returned against Denmark during the 1807 attack on Copenhagen.

evidence.note: Danish-Norwegian losses remain uncertain at roughly 1,100 to 2,200, against 963 British killed and wounded; Britain captured twelve ships, burned eleven for lack of prize crews, and retained Holstein as HMS Nassau.

segments.summary: Danish-Norwegian losses remain uncertain because many volunteers lacked naval experience, while Britain recorded 963 killed and wounded and destroyed most captured Danish ships.

segments.title: Paul's death ends the diplomatic crisis
segments.body: The League was tied so closely to Paul I that news of his assassination gave Denmark room to negotiate without openly rupturing relations with Russia. During the talks, Danish officials sometimes spoke French on the assumption that British officers could not follow them, only to find that Nelson understood the language. A settlement was reached, after which Parker sailed toward Karlskrona and induced the Swedish fleet to return to port. His reluctance to push farther into the eastern Baltic led Britain to recall him with honour and transfer command to Nelson. Nelson's handling of the Danish truce had also shown that he could conduct the diplomacy needed to finish the campaign. He then advanced to Reval while leaving ships to watch Sweden. By the time he arrived, the thawed Russian fleet had departed for Kronstadt and negotiations to end the League were already under way, making further action unnecessary.

evidence.note: Paul I's assassination opened Danish negotiations and dissolved the League's purpose; Parker was recalled after moving only as far as Karlskrona, while Nelson reached Reval after the Russian fleet had left and peace talks were under way.

segments.summary: News of Tsar Paul's assassination allowed Denmark to regard the League as finished, settle with Britain, and end the Baltic operation before a wider fleet war developed.

segments.title: Remembering naval historian James Goldrick
segments.body: James Goldrick is remembered for both his scholarship and his generosity. He made time for younger historians and encouraged newcomers at naval and maritime history conferences, including through discussions such as Bilge Pumps. At a Greenwich conference, he eased the pressure on a young speaker with a joke about blaming the professor if the talk went badly. The tribute holds that later generations can produce new leading scholars without replacing the distinctive kindness and mentorship of those who have died. This moment shows how the naval-history community sustains itself through encouragement as well as published research.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke remembers James Goldrick's scholarship, mentorship, humour, and influence on younger naval historians.

segments.summary: The closing tribute remembers James Goldrick as an exceptional naval historian who welcomed and encouraged younger scholars.
